newsitem.title: USA: Compaq on deal spree but rumors discounted.
newsitem.headline: Compaq on deal spree but rumors discounted.

text.p: Compaq Computer Corp's deal to buy Microcom Inc Thursday exemplifies the kind of strategic deals the PC giant will continue to make with its big cash pile, as it seeks to be more than just a PC maker.

At the same time, rumors have been swirling in the market this week that Compaq was in talks to acquire a direct seller of PCs, Micron Electronics Inc. Analysts said another recent rumor was that Compaq talked to another direct PC firm, Gateway 2000 Inc, a few months ago about a deal.
But they said it is unlikely Compaq would buy either firm.

Analysts said that the rumors have likely crept up because Compaq has said that it is moving to embrace a build-to-order manufacturing strategy to address some of its business, a technique successfully adopted by direct marketers of PCs such as Gateway and Dell Computer Corp.
They said that because Compaq now has a cash pile of about $4 billion, as of fourth quarter, the PC maker is looking to do strategic acquisitions with some of it.
"Clearly Compaq has the cash, they have a whole organization looking at acquisitions," said John Dean, a Salomon Brothers analyst.

But Dean and other analysts said that Compaq's $280 million pact for Microcom, a developer of remote access technologies and modems, fits more with Compaq's strategy to offer more to customers than just PCs and servers.
"They want to be a major enterprise company," Dean added. "They have a lot of piece parts so they have to go out and find things that will tie them all together."

Analysts said the Microcom deal fits this bill because Compaq will be able to provide remote access capabilities and modems with products called remote access servers, which are in great demand by Internet access providers.
Other acquisitions by Compaq were also in the networking area, to add to its portfolio of products it can offer a corporation to help it build its network infrastructure.

Analysts said that Compaq is under some pressure from Dell and Gateway and less from Micron, all of whom sell their systems directly to customers, through mail and phone orders. These companies have built up manufacturing systems where they can build-to-order, and they don't have the added costs that Compaq has by going through distributors or resellers.
"(Compaq) will set up their own organization," said Daniel Ries, a Nomura Research analyst.

"(Direct sales) will only be a small portion of their sales," Ries said, adding that Compaq will continue to sell PCs, servers and other products through resellers, who reach the samll to medium corporate market which relies on resellers for servicing, maintenance.

He said Compaq is also developing a build-to-order model for its resellers, not just for direct sales. Compaq said it is creating a configure-to-order program at its Houston manufacturing site for its resllers and its customers, a move that will translate into lower prices and increased demand.
A Compaq spokeswoman declined to comment on merger rumors.

Gateway 2000 did not return calls seeking comment and Micron Electronics declined to comment on rumors. Micron Electronics is majority owned by Micron Technology Inc, the memory chip maker, which owns about 65 percent.
On Wednesday, PC Week Online reported that Micron Technology has held preliminary discussions to sell Micron Electronics business to Compaq, Hewlett-Packard Co, Sanyo Electric, Gateway 2000.
Analysts said Micron Electronics could be up for sale, but it is not a match for Compaq. "Micron is too small to benefit Compaq," said Louis Mazzucchelli of Gerard Klauer Mattison.
